newsitem.title: GERMANY: German retailers say sales to stagnate in 1996. [CORRECTED 13:54 GMT]
newsitem.headline: German retailers say sales to stagnate in 1996. [CORRECTED 13:54 GMT]

text.p: German retailers expect turnover to stagnate this year despite an overall economic recovery, the head of the HDE retailers association said on Wednesday.
HDE chief Holger Wenzel told reporters that sales in the first half of 1996 were flat and he did not anticipate a pickup after the phasing in of longer shopping hours from November.

Real retail turnover has not grown in four years and the extension of Germany's notoriously restrictive shop hours has triggered a series of wildcat strikes by store unions seeking extra compensation for late working.

Pay agreements have been struck in a handful of states, but deals are proving elusive elsewhere. Workers walked out of five stores in Hesse on Wednesday to back their wage demands and unions said they planned further stoppages.

Wenzel said that the longer opening hours would result in a shift of retail business from the high street to big shopping centres. Only 10 to 15 percent of stores would actually opt to keep their doors open much later.
Around 35 percent of retailers suffered falls in first half turnover of over 2.5 percent, while just 15 percent posted gains of over 2.5 percent, Wenzel said.

He added that the consumer hesitancy resulted from growing worries that Germany's long post-war climb in living standards could soon come to an end and that the social security net would be dismantled.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservative coalition government is seeking to pass an austerity package this autumn which will impose 50 (corrects figure from 70) billion marks ($33 billion) in spending cuts and slash 20 billion marks from the social welfare budget.
-- Douglas Busvine, Bonn newsroom, 49 228 26097150 ($ = 1.512 German Marks)
